problem.title: Inspection Pairs
problem.statement: Ari, Bea, and Chen are available. Two different people are chosen to inspect a campsite together. They have the same role. How many different inspection pairs are possible?
hints: Count first-name, second-name descriptions before removing order.
Ari-Bea and Bea-Ari describe the same equal-role pair.

solutionSteps.title: Count ordered descriptions
solutionSteps.body: There are 3 choices for the first listed person and 2 choices for the second, giving 3 × 2 = 6 descriptions.

solutionSteps.title: Bundle the same outcomes
solutionSteps.body: Each inspection pair has 2! = 2 name orders, and swapping the names does not change the pair.

solutionSteps.title: Count pairs
solutionSteps.body: The six descriptions form three equal, non-overlapping bundles, so 6 ÷ 2 = 3 pairs.

validationMethods: exhaustive enumeration of Ari-Bea, Ari-Chen, and Bea-Chen
notes: Both independent methods give exactly 3 inspection pairs.

problem.title: Gallery Wall
problem.statement: A gallery owns 6 distinct posters and will display 3 of them on one wall. The arrangement on the wall is decided later and does not count as part of the selection. How many different sets of 3 posters can the gallery select?
hints: First count ordered selections of three distinct posters.
How many selection orders describe each same set of three?

solutionSteps.title: Count ordered selections
solutionSteps.body: There are 6 choices, then 5, then 4, for 6 × 5 × 4 = 120 ordered descriptions.

solutionSteps.title: Find the bundle size
solutionSteps.body: Each fixed set of three posters can be selected in 3! = 6 orders.

solutionSteps.title: Count the sets
solutionSteps.body: The 120 descriptions partition into bundles of six, so 120 ÷ 6 = 20 sets.

validationMethods: independent complement enumeration C(6,3)=20 via the 20 three-element subsets
answer-choice uniqueness audit and manual novelty review
notes: All three calculations give 20; arrangement is explicitly excluded from the outcome.

problem.title: Seven Greetings
problem.statement: Seven people each shake hands once with every other person. How many handshakes occur?
hints: Count a named first person and a different named second person.
A-to-B and B-to-A describe the same handshake.

solutionSteps.title: Count directed descriptions
solutionSteps.body: Seven first-person choices and six second-person choices give 7 × 6 = 42 directed descriptions.

solutionSteps.title: Remove direction
solutionSteps.body: Each actual handshake appears in exactly 2! = 2 directions.

notes: Both methods count each mutual handshake once and give 21.

problem.title: Festival Planning Team
problem.statement: From 6 volunteers, a 4-person festival planning team is chosen. Then one team member is named chair and a different team member is named recorder. How many different team-and-officer outcomes are possible?
hints: Within a fixed team, chair and recorder are different roles.

solutionSteps.title: Choose the team
solutionSteps.body: Choosing 4 of 6 volunteers without order gives C(6,4) = 15 teams.

solutionSteps.title: Assign the officers
solutionSteps.body: Within any fixed team, there are 4 choices for chair and then 3 for recorder, giving 12 assignments.

solutionSteps.title: Multiply the stages
solutionSteps.body: Each of the 15 teams permits each of 12 assignments, so 15 × 12 = 180 outcomes.

notes: The independent count chooses chair and recorder first, then two additional role-free members.

problem.title: Three-Symbol Codes
problem.statement: A display has 8 distinct symbols. A code uses 3 different symbols in order, with no repetition. How many codes are possible?
hints: First choose which three symbols appear.
Then restore the 3! orders of each chosen set because code positions matter.

solutionSteps.title: Choose the symbols
solutionSteps.body: There are C(8,3) = 56 sets of three symbols.

solutionSteps.title: Arrange each set
solutionSteps.body: Each chosen set produces 3! = 6 different ordered codes.

solutionSteps.title: Count and check
solutionSteps.body: Thus 56 × 6 = 336. Directly filling positions also gives 8 × 7 × 6 = 336.

notes: The two methods independently confirm 336 and expose the inverse relationship between choosing and arranging.
